content: 1. Epidemicand pandemic-prone acute respiratory infections can spread through contact transmission. This occurs when a susceptible host comes into physical contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. Direct contact transmission involves body-to-body surface contact and the physical transfer of microorganisms between an infected or colonized person and a susceptible host, such as through contaminated hands. 2. Disinfection is a process that eliminates all viable pathogenic microorganisms, except bacterial spores, from inanimate objects. 3. Droplet transmission refers to the spread of infectious agents through droplets generated by an infected person during coughing, sneezing, or talking. These droplets, which contain microorganisms, are typically propelled less than 1 meter through the air and deposited on the mucosa of the eyes, mouth, nose, throat, or pharynx of another person. Most droplets are large, travel short distances, and do not remain suspended in the air, so special air handling and ventilation are not required to prevent droplet transmission. 4. Environmental ventilation can be categorized into three types: Mechanical ventilation uses fans to introduce or exhaust outdoor or treated recycled air into or out of a building or room. Natural ventilation relies on natural forces, such as wind pressure or pressure differences due to air density, to introduce and distribute outdoor air into a building. Mixed-mode ventilation combines mechanical and natural ventilation. 5. Ventilation flow rates can be measured as absolute ventilation flow rates in liters per second (L/s) or liters per second per cubic meter (L/s/m³), or as air changes per hour (ACH) relative to the volume of the space. Ventilation rate refers to the absolute amount of inflow air per unit time, while air change rate refers to the relative amount of inflow air per unit time. 6. Hand hygiene encompasses handwashing, antiseptic handwashing, antiseptic hand rubbing, and surgical hand antisepsis. 7. A health-care facility is any establishment that provides direct patient care, such as hospitals, outpatient clinics, or home care settings. Health personnel include anyone employed or contracted to provide health services, such as medical practitioners, nurses, therapists, social workers, pharmacists, and spiritual counselors. 8. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is a practical discipline aimed at preventing healthcare-associated infections. It is a critical component of healthcare infrastructure, designed to protect patients, healthcare workers, visitors, and others in healthcare settings. IPC also prepares facilities for early detection and management of epidemics, contributes to controlling community-acquired infectious diseases, prevents the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance, and minimizes the environmental impact of infections and their management. 9. Infectious respiratory aerosols are particles containing infectious agents. Their size is influenced by factors such as the force of generation, environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity, airflow), and the size of the organisms within the droplets. Larger particles settle quickly within 1 meter of the source, while smaller particles evaporate rapidly, leaving dried residues that remain airborne for varying durations. 10. Isolation precautions are measures to reduce the risk of infection transmission. These include: Standard Precautions, which apply to all patient care. Additional Precautions, which are required in specific circumstances and include Contact, Droplet, and Airborne Precautions. 11. Respiratory hygiene involves covering the mouth and nose during coughing or sneezing (e.g., using a mask, tissue, sleeve, or elbow) and performing hand hygiene afterward to reduce the spread of respiratory secretions containing infectious particles. 12. Spatial separation refers to maintaining a physical distance of at least 1 meter between patients or between patients and healthcare workers, either within a confined space or between separate areas such as rooms or wards. 13. Special measures involve grouping patients with the same suspected diagnosis in designated units or wards when the causative agent has not been laboratory-confirmed. 14. A medical mask, also known as a surgical or procedure mask, is a type of personal protective equipment designed to protect healthcare workers from droplet-transmitted pathogens or to shield them during activities likely to generate splashes or sprays of blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions. 15. A new influenza virus refers to a strain of influenza that has not previously circulated in humans. These viruses, often of swine or avian origin, have the potential to spread among humans, such as H5 and H7 strains of avian influenza, most notably A(H5N1). 16. A pandemic is an epidemic that occurs worldwide or across multiple countries, affecting a large number of people. 17. A particulate respirator, also known as a filtering facepiece respirator, is a type of facial mask that uses a filter as part of the facepiece or is entirely composed of filtering material, designed to seal tightly to the face. 18. Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality from infectious diseases globally, particularly affecting the youngest and oldest populations in lowand middle-income nations. These infections, often caused by viruses or mixed viral-bacterial pathogens, are highly contagious and can spread rapidly. 19. Infection prevention and control measures in healthcare settings are essential for patient and worker safety, as well as for managing communicable disease threats. Basic IPC precautions, such as Standard Precautions, are fundamental to safe healthcare delivery. 20. The management of ARIs requires early identification, prompt isolation precautions, proper patient placement, and adequate ventilation to contain and mitigate the impact of pathogens that pose significant public health threats. 21. These guidelines focus on non-pharmacological IPC measures for ARIs in healthcare settings, targeting IPC professionals, healthcare managers, policymakers, and healthcare workers. They emphasize a syndromic and epidemiological approach to assessing infection risks and applying additional IPC measures, particularly for ARIs that may present as epidemics or pandemics. 22. Leadership in healthcare facilities is crucial to ensure a culture of safety and consistent application of IPC measures during outbreaks and at all other times. 23. The guidelines recommend maintaining additional precautions for patients with ARIs for the duration of symptomatic illness, vaccinating healthcare workers caring for high-risk patients, and avoiding routine antiviral prophylaxis for healthcare workers exposed to ARIs.
